## Definition

Use the flat oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski model, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and SI convention $x^0=ct$ of [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. A **relativistic-particle-mechanics collision configuration** is a mass-specified causal collision datum of [[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: an event $p\in A$, a finite nonempty incoming list $P_1,\ldots,P_N\in V$, and a finite nonempty outgoing list $P'_1,\ldots,P'_K\in V$, where every leg is a nonzero future-causal vector in the same displacement space $V$. A massive leg has a recorded mass $m>0$ and the massive-sector momentum of [[def-rpm-mechanical-momentum-and-observer-energy]]; a null leg has recorded mass $0$ and is a nonzero future-null vector with its scale specified independently. The definition does not identify a null momentum with $mU$ at $m=0$.

The side totals are the finite vector sums $Q_{\rm in}:=\sum_{i=1}^N P_i$ and $Q_{\rm out}:=\sum_{j=1}^K P'_j$. All legs are attached to the same event, so the sums compare vectors in one affine displacement space; no transport between different events is part of the datum. The adjective **isolated** is reserved for a model condition used by the postulate below: no external four-momentum transfer during the idealized event and no omitted incoming or outgoing leg.

At an event, an **observer** is a future unit timelike vector $n$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and its rest space is $n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. Observer energy $E_n(P):=-c\eta(P,n)$ and spatial momentum $q_n(P):=P+\eta(P,n)n\in n^\perp$ are those of [[def-rpm-mechanical-momentum-and-observer-energy]]. Their units are joules and kilogram metres per second. An inertial laboratory means one named inertial chart and its time-axis observer; it is not a general observer congruence or an arbitrary coordinate chart.

## Definition

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Fix a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,T)$ with signature $(-+++)$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Here $T$ denotes the supplied smooth timelike field selecting the future cone, called $N$ in that geometric definition. Use the distinction among a spacetime, a worldline, a pointwise observer, an observer congruence, a tetrad and a chart given in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. This definition does not make $g$ dynamical.

In this relativistic-particle model, $m>0$ is a fixed **primitive mass parameter** measured in kilograms, and $c>0$ is a fixed **primitive conversion parameter** measured in metres per second. They are parameters of the adopted physical formulation, not quantities derived by this definition. Coordinates $x^a$ in an SI chart have length units; a cotangent vector $p=p_a\,dx^a$ has units of momentum, $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, when all four coordinates are in metres. The canonical one-form $p_a\,dx^a$ therefore has action units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Along a future-directed timelike curve with tangent $V=dx/d\lambda$, set $s:=\sqrt{-g(V,V)}$; then $d\tau=s\,d\lambda/c$, independently of the increasing regular parameter. The length action $-mc\int s\,d\lambda$ has action units. For a future unit observer $n$ and future causal covector $p$, define the model normal-observer energy and spatial momentum covector by

$$E_n(p):=-c\,p(n),\qquad q_n(p):=p+p(n)n^\flat,$$

where $n^\flat=g(n,\cdot)$. The restriction of $g^{-1}$ to covectors annihilating $n$ is positive definite, so it supplies the norm of $q_n(p)$. These are quantity definitions and unit conventions; they do not identify canonical momentum with mechanical momentum, assert that an apparatus measured these values, or establish a dynamical law.

## Definition

Let $(P,\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold with its induced Poisson bracket, and let $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ be a regular constraint family on a common zero surface $N=\{z:\chi_a(z)=0\}$ as defined by [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. The family is **first-class on $N$** when

$$\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}(z)=0\qquad\text{for every }z\in N\text{ and all }a,b.$$

Equivalently, each pairwise bracket is weakly zero in the notation $F\approx0$ of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. The Poisson bracket convention is that of [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]. This definition is a pointwise closure condition on the stated regular surface; it does not assert multiplier-algorithm termination or global quotient regularity.

## Definition

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-+++)$, with the geometric meaning fixed by [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Here $T$ denotes the future-cone field called $N$ in that definition. A **temporal product chart** is a smooth coordinate map from an open product $I\times\Omega\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ onto an open subset of $M$, with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$. We require $x^0$ to have length units and each $x^i$ to have length units in the physical interpretation.

The chart has **lapse-shift data** $(N,\beta,h)$ when $N:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$, $\beta^i:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $h_{ij}:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, $h_{ij}=h_{ji}$, and the matrix $(h_{ij})$ is positive definite at each point, with

$$g=-N^2(dx^0)^2+h_{ij}(dx^i+\beta^i dx^0)(dx^j+\beta^j dx^0).$$

Write $h^{ij}$ for the inverse matrix. The normal field is

$$n=N^{-1}(\partial_0-\beta^i\partial_i).$$

Direct contraction gives $g(n,n)=-1$; require that $n$ is future-directed in the supplied time orientation. This field of observers is distinct from the coordinate vector $\partial_0$, which may be spacelike. The coefficients $N,\beta^i,h_{ij}$ are dimensionless when all four coordinates are in metres. This definition is local to the specified product chart; it asserts no global temporal foliation.

## Definition

Let $m,c,\kappa>0$, let $x,p\in\mathbb R^3$, and set

$$D:=(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R^3,\qquad r:=|x|,\qquad \mathcal E(p):=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|p|^2}.$$

The **repulsive relativistic Coulomb Hamiltonian** is

$$H(x,p):=\mathcal E(p)+\frac{\kappa}{r},$$

and its **phase system** is the autonomous ODE on the open set $D$

$$\dot x=\nabla_pH=\frac{c^2p}{\mathcal E(p)},\qquad \dot p=-\nabla_xH=\frac{\kappa x}{r^3}.$$

Here the system parameter $t$ is time in seconds and dot denotes $d/dt$; $m$ is a positive mass parameter (kilograms in the SI interpretation), $c$ a positive speed parameter (metres per second), and $\kappa$ a positive energy-times-length parameter (joule-metres). Define the radial momentum $p_r:=x\cdot p/r$ and angular-momentum vector $J:=x\times p$. A trajectory is a $C^1$ solution of this ODE on an interval; maximality is in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]].

This is only a mathematical phase system. Its physical interpretation as a charged particle in an externally prescribed Coulomb field requires separate model assumptions.

## Definition

Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

## Definition

Use the dimensionless coordinates, simple configurations, and pair potential of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. A sequence $(\Lambda_k)_{k\geq1}$ of bounded measurable regions is van Hove if $|\Lambda_k|\to\infty$ and, for every fixed $s>0$,
$$\frac{|\{x\in\Lambda_k:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda_k)\leq s\}|}{|\Lambda_k|}\longrightarrow0.$$
This is an explicit condition on the boundary-layer volume; increasing volume alone does not imply it. A free wall permits particles only in $\Lambda_k$ and includes no exterior particles. A periodic wall uses the specified periodic cell and its image convention.

For the deterministic exterior class, let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and $\Lambda_n=[-n-1/2,n+1/2)^d$, with $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$. For a locally finite exterior configuration $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$, write $N_{C+i}(\zeta)=|\zeta\cap(C+i)|$. Given $t<\infty$, define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C+i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\ \text{for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$, its exterior interaction is
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)=\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n}\varphi(x-y),$$
interpreted as an extended-real sum. A positive infinite value has zero Boltzmann weight. The regular tail controls distant terms; the class $\Omega(t)$ is a fixed uniform bound on exterior cell counts, not permission for an arbitrary volume-filling external potential. The van Hove and uniformly tempered exterior conditions are separate boundary regimes.

## Postulate

Adopt the unlabelled positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$ obtained from labelled tuples by dividing by permutation multiplicity. Thus, for every nonnegative measurable symmetric function $f$ on $\Lambda^N$,
$$\int f(\omega)\,\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda^N}f(\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\})\,d^{dN}x.$$
The reference coordinates and length scale are those of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. This convention treats two labelled lists that differ only by a particle permutation as the same positional state. The factor $1/N!$ is an adopted indistinguishable-particle measure convention for this classical model, not a theorem that classical trajectories or every classical description must use quotient states.

For later comparison, define the unit-intensity Poisson reference on a finite region by
$$Q_\Lambda(d\omega)=e^{-|\Lambda|}\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega).$$
Its total mass is one because $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$ has total mass $|\Lambda|^N/N!$ and $e^{-|\Lambda|}\sum_{N\geq0}|\Lambda|^N/N!=1$. This is a positional reference measure in the chosen dimensionless coordinates; it supplies no empirical claim about particle trajectories.

## Definition

Use the periodic boxes $\Lambda_n$ and positional energy of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], and the exact-$N$ measure $\mu_{\Lambda_n,N}$ of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. Given $N_n\in\mathbb N$, a reduced configuration-energy center $e\in\mathbb R$ joules per dimensionless reference volume, and a width $\delta_n>0$ in the same units, define
$$S_n(N_n,e,\delta_n)=\{\omega\subset\Lambda_n:|\omega|=N_n,\ |H_{N_n}^{\mathrm{per}}(\omega)/V_n-e|\leq\delta_n\}.$$
When $0<\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(S_n)<\infty$, the uniform positional shell law is
$$M_n(A)=\frac{\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(A\cap S_n)}{\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(S_n)}.$$
A shrinking energy-density shell uses some specified sequence $\delta_n\downarrow0$. Its total energy width is $2\delta_nV_n$, which is $o(V_n)$ but need not be microscopic or bounded. Existence of a normalizing shell and the existence of a suitable shrinking sequence are separate theorem obligations. This is not a surface measure on an exact-energy hypersurface and not a phase-space shell for $K(p)+H_N^{\mathrm{per}}$.

## Definition

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\iota(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

## Statement

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite-support nonnegative compound maps, equal-mass comparisons, and A1–A6.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the compound relation is reflexive and transitive, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, and satisfies the stated fixed-spectator stability axiom. It does not assume CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their total coefficient masses add under composition and scale under nonnegative dilation. [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] also proves that zero mass is equivalent to the empty map; the spectator need not have the same mass as either base.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite-support maps $u,v$, $u\preceq_s v$ means $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$, with common signed translation leaving the difference unchanged.

## Proof

1.1 Assume $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\prec B/n+C/n$. Define $E_j=(n-j)A/n+jB/n+C/n$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$. For $j<n$, add the common spectator $(n-j-1)A/n+jB/n$ to the scaled comparison to obtain $E_j\prec E_{j+1}$. Transitivity yields $A+C/n=E_0\prec E_n=B+C/n$. Stability with bases $A,B$, fixed positive spectators $C,C$, and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity gives $C=0$ and the implication is immediate. Conversely, consistency gives $A+C\prec B+C$ from $A\prec B$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. The same finite-sum argument proves closure under addition; reflexivity follows from reflexivity of the zero compound. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open convex domain, finite-valued function, and Euclidean norm.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: line segments and finite convex combinations of points in a convex set remain in that set.

## Proof

1.1 Choose a closed cube centered at $x_0$ whose concentric dilation by factor $2$ lies in $U$. Every point of the cube is a convex combination of its finitely many vertices, so [F1] and convexity bound $f$ above there by the largest vertex value $M$. If $x$ lies in the cube, then $2x_0-x$ lies in the dilated cube; convexity gives $f(x_0)\le(f(x)+f(2x_0-x))/2$, hence $f(x)\ge2f(x_0)-M'$, where $M'$ is the finite upper bound on the dilated cube. Thus $f$ is bounded above and below on a ball about $x_0$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Choose concentric balls $B(x_0,r)\subset B(x_0,2r)\subset U$ on which $m\le f\le M$. For distinct $x,y\in B(x_0,r/2)$, extend the segment from $x$ through $y$ to $z=y+(r/2)(y-x)/\|y-x\|$, which lies in $B(x_0,2r)$. Put $\theta=\|y-x\|/(r/2+\|y-x\|)$, so $y=(1-\theta)x+\theta z$. Convexity yields $f(y)-f(x)\le\theta(M-m)\le(2(M-m)/r)\|y-x\|$. Repeating with $x,y$ interchanged gives the reverse bound. Negation proves the concave case. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty convex $C\subseteq H$ in finite dimension. Affine dimension is the dimension of its translation space.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: every finite convex combination of points of $C$ belongs to $C$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $k=\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a singleton and is open in its affine hull. If $k>0$, the definition of affine hull supplies $k+1$ affinely independent points of $C$ spanning it. Their simplex lies in $C$ by [F1]. Its barycenter has all $k+1$ barycentric coordinates positive; sufficiently small coordinate perturbations preserve positivity and their sum one. Thus a relative neighborhood of that barycenter lies in the simplex, proving $\operatorname{ri}_H C\ne\varnothing$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Fix $w,y,t$ as in the Statement. The case $t=0$ is $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$. Suppose $0<t<1$ and put $q=(1-t)w+ty$. Choose $r>0$ so the relative ball $B_H(w,r)$ lies in $C$. Since $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, choose $y_m\in C$ converging to $y$. For any $q'$ in a sufficiently small relative ball about $q$, the point $w_m(q'):=(q'-ty_m)/(1-t)$ lies in $B_H(w,r)$ once that ball is chosen and then $m$ is large. Hence $q'=(1-t)w_m(q')+ty_m\in C$ by [F1]. A relative neighborhood of $q$ lies in $C$, so $q\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$. [given, F1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on a nonempty open convex domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 include consistency, scaling, splitting, convex-combination access, and stability for positive spectators.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: a nonempty convex set has nonempty relative interior, and segments from a relative-interior point to a closure point, excluding the closure endpoint, remain in the relative interior.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: any finite common spectator cancels when the two bases have equal mass, under A1–A6 without CH.

## Proof

1.1 If $x\prec y$ and $x\prec z$, splitting gives $x\sim(tx,(1-t)x)$. Consistency, positive scaling, and transitivity then give $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(ty,(1-t)z)\prec ty+(1-t)z$, so the convex combination belongs to $A_x$. [A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $y=tx+(1-t)z$ with $0<t<1$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$. Splitting gives $y\sim(ty,(1-t)y)$. If $y\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $ty$ gives $(ty,(1-t)y)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. Compose and cancel the common $(1-t)z$ by [F2], then scale by $1/t$, to get $x\prec y$. If instead $x\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $tx$ gives $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$; recombination gives $x\prec y$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Take $y\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. If $y\in A_x$, the claim is immediate. Otherwise choose $w\in\operatorname{ri} A_x$ by [F1]. Because $\Gamma_i$ is open, choose $z=w+(1+\eta)(y-w)\in\Gamma_i$ for some $\eta>0$. For every integer $n>1+\eta$, $y_n=(1+1/n)y-z/n=w+(1-\eta/n)(y-w)$ lies in $\operatorname{ri}A_x$ by [F1], so $x\prec y_n$. Also $y=\frac{n}{n+1}y_n+\frac1{n+1}z$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(\frac n{n+1}y_n,\frac1{n+1}z)\prec y$; scaling by $(n+1)/n$ and using the reversible split of $y$ gives $(y_n,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Consistency adds the same spectator $z/n$ to $x\prec y_n$, and transitivity with step 2.1 gives $(x,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$ for every $n>1+\eta$. Apply the stability hypothesis in [A1] to bases $x,y$, fixed positive equal-mass represented spectators $z,y$, and the tail sequence $\epsilon_m=1/(m+n_0)$ with $n_0>1+\eta$. It follows that $x\prec y$. Thus every relative closure point belongs to $A_x$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonnegative continuous function and the stated integral inequality.

[F1] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

[F2] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: the product rule, chain rule, and mean value theorem apply to the displayed differentiable real functions.

[F3] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $(e^x)'=e^x$ for every real $x$.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], the integral defining $h(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ exists. Continuity of $f$ gives $h'(t)=f(t)$ on $(0,T)$: the difference quotient error is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|r|}|f(s)-f(t)|$, which tends to zero as $r\to0$. Also $h$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. The hypothesis gives $h'\le Lh$, so [F2]–[F3] yield $g'(t)\le0$ for $g(t)=e^{-Lt}h(t)$ on $(0,T)$. The mean value theorem makes $g$ nonincreasing; since $g(0)=0$ and $g\ge0$, $g\equiv0$ and $h\equiv0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For any $t>0$, the nonnegative continuous function $f$ has integral $h(t)=0$. If $f(t_0)>0$ at any $t_0>0$, continuity gives a positive lower bound on a nonempty subinterval of $[0,t_0]$, contradicting $h(t_0)=0$. At $t=0$ the assumed inequality gives $f(0)\le0$; nonnegativity gives $f(0)=0$. Hence $f\equiv0$. [step 1.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space and convex set.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex Euclidean set is strictly separated from that set by a nonzero linear functional.

[F2] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F3] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: Euclidean coordinates identify linear functionals with vectors and give the usual unit sphere.

## Proof

1.1 Choose affine coordinates identifying $H$ with $\mathbb R^k$. Convexity of $C$ makes its closure $K$ convex: approximate any two points of $K$ by sequences in $C$ and pass to the limit in each convex combination. Since $z\in\partial_H K$, choose $z_m\notin K$ with $z_m\to z$. By [F1], for each $m$ there are $u_m\ne0$ and $c_m$ with $u_m\cdot q\le c_m<u_m\cdot z_m$ for all $q\in K$. Normalize $u_m$ to unit length; [F3] places these vectors on the compact unit sphere, which is compact by [F2], so a subsequence converges to a unit vector $u$. [F2] and [F3] provide the convergent subsequence. [given, F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 For every $q\in K$, the inequalities give $u_m\cdot(q-z_m)<0$. Along the convergent subsequence, continuity of the Euclidean inner product yields $u\cdot(q-z)\le0$. The limit vector has unit length, so its functional is nonzero and supports $K$, hence $C$, at $z$. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, its orthogonal complement has dimension at least two. Choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on an open convex $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=n_i+1$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each sector is supported at every state by exactly one hyperplane, and every state has a strict successor.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$; if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$ by transitivity.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at its relative boundary in its affine hull, and a set of affine dimension at most $d-2$ has at least two distinct ambient supports through each of its points.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: a convex set has nonempty relative interior, and every segment from a relative-interior point to a closure point, except for the closure endpoint, stays in the relative interior.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $A_x$ has empty ambient interior. If $d=1$, S1 supplies a strict successor $y\ne x$; convexity puts the nondegenerate interval between $x$ and $y$ in $A_x$, contradicting empty interior. Thus take $d\ge2$. The affine hull of $A_x$ has dimension at most $d-1$. If its dimension were at most $d-2$, [F2] would give two distinct supporting hyperplanes at $x$, contradicting S2. Hence its affine hull is a hyperplane $H$; this $H$ supports $A_x$ at every point, including $x$. [A1, F2]

1.2 By S1 choose $y$ with $x\prec\prec y$. Then $y\in A_x$ and $x\notin A_y$. Transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x\subseteq H$. If $A_y$ had affine dimension at most $d-2$, [F2] would again give multiple ambient supports at $y$, contrary to S2. Thus $\operatorname{aff}A_y=H$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.3 Choose $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H A_y$ by [F3]. The segment from $w$ to $x$ is contained in $H\cap\Gamma_i$ by convexity of both sets, starts in $A_y$, and ends outside $A_y$. Its intersection with $A_y$ is closed by relative closedness [F1], so it has a last point $z$ before $x$. Points immediately after $z$ on this segment lie outside $A_y$ and, because $A_y$ is closed in the open set $\Gamma_i$, outside $\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. Thus $z\in\partial_H\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. The support statement [F2] supplies a nonzero functional on $H$ whose zero hyperplane supports $A_y$ at $z$. [F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 Extend this functional to the ambient Euclidean space by taking its normal vector in the direction space of $H$. Its zero hyperplane contains the within-$H$ support and is not $H$ itself. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y$, so the extended plane supports $A_z$ at $z$; the plane $H$ also supports $A_z$. These are distinct, contradicting S2 at $z$. Therefore $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior. [A1, F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be closed and convex with nonempty interior, $d\ge1$, and let $x\in\partial K$. Suppose $K$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$. Choose its inward unit normal $n$, so $n\cdot(q-x)\ge0$ for every $q\in K$. Then for every $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$ for every $0<t<\delta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The closed convex set, boundary point, unique supporting hyperplane, and Euclidean inner product.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex Euclidean set admits a strict separating linear functional.

[F2] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: Euclidean linear functionals are represented by vectors.

[F3] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F4] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: finite convex combinations of points in a convex set remain in it.



## Proof

1.1 Let $T=\overline{\{a(q-x):a\ge0,\ q\in K\}}$. This is a closed convex cone. If a nonzero functional $\ell$ is nonnegative on $T$, then it is nonnegative on $K-x$, so its zero plane through $x$ supports $K$. Uniqueness in the hypothesis makes that plane the plane with normal $n$; the inward sign forces $\ell=c n\cdot(\,\cdot\,)$ for some $c>0$. [given, F2]

2.1 The support at $x$ gives $T\subseteq\{w:n\cdot w\ge0\}$. If $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$ were outside $T$, strict separation [F1] of $v$ from the cone would give a nonzero functional $\ell$ nonnegative on $T$ and negative at $v$: the separating bound is zero because $0\in T$ and $T$ is a cone. Step 1.1 then makes $\ell$ a positive multiple of $n$, contradicting $n\cdot v>0$. Thus the open half-space $n\cdot w>0$ lies in $T$, and each such $v$ is an interior point of $T$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix such $v$. Since $v\in\operatorname{int}T$, choose $d+1$ affinely independent vectors in a small ball about $v$ whose simplex contains a neighborhood of $v$. Approximate each vector by a nonzero cone generator $g_j=a_j(q_j-x)$ with $a_j>0$, $q_j\in K$. Sufficiently close approximations preserve affine independence and keep $v$ in the simplex interior, so a neighborhood $N$ of $v$ lies in the simplex of the $g_j$. For each $w\in N$, write $w=\sum_j\theta_j(w)a_j(q_j-x)$ with $\theta_j(w)\ge0$ and $\sum_j\theta_j(w)=1$. Shrink $N$ so its closure is a closed bounded neighborhood of $v$ contained in that simplex. Barycentric coordinates vary continuously there; by [F3] the closure is compact, so $A:=\sup_{w\in N}\sum_j\theta_j(w)a_j<\infty$. [step 2.1, construct, F2, F3]

4.1 Choose $\delta>0$ with $\delta A<1$. For $0<t<\delta$ and each $w\in N$, $x+tw=(1-t\sum_j\theta_j a_j)x+\sum_j t\theta_j a_j q_j$ is a convex combination of points of $K$, hence lies in $K$ by [F4]. Therefore $x+tN\subset K$, so a neighborhood of $x+tv$ lies in $K$ and $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$. [step 3.1, given, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on an open convex simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each $A_x$ is supported at $x$ by a unique finite-slope plane; $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$, and its collinear order implications hold.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at each relative boundary point of its closure in its affine hull.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-unique-support-inward-ray]]: at a full-dimensional convex set's boundary point with a unique support, every direction strictly toward the supporting half-space's interior enters the set's interior for all sufficiently small positive steps.

[F5] [[lem-tdmath-convex-function-local-lipschitz]]: every finite convex function on an open convex set is locally Lipschitz.

[F6] [[lem-tdmath-integral-zero-uniqueness]]: a nonnegative continuous function bounded by a constant times its zero-start integral is identically zero.

[F7] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F8] [[thm-chain-rule]]: the derivative of a composition of differentiable maps is the composition of their derivatives.

[F9] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: a continuous function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior with an integrable derivative extension, has endpoint increment equal to the integral of that derivative.

[F10] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F10]. Write a support plane's inward unit normal with energy component nonzero, as ensured by its finite-slope form.

1.1 For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side. [A1, F1, F4]

1.2 The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant. [A1, F2, F3, F4]

1.3 Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain. [A1, F6, F8, F9, F10, given, construct]

2.1 The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. The nested compact intervals have a common limit point $x_\infty\in\Gamma_i$ by [F7], and their lengths tend to zero. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side. [A1, F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 4.1]

6.1 For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative. [A1, F1, F5, step 5.1]

7.1 If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$. [A1, F1, step 6.1, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the component charts are open, represented states have their positive type weights, and the relation is composition-consistent and transitive.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1 sends every admissible split to its join; T2 supplies, for each join state, at least one admissible split accessible in both directions to that join state, at the same summed energy and work coordinates.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each component domain has a constant sign $\varepsilon_\Gamma$ with fixed-work comparison equivalent to $\varepsilon_\Gamma(u_y-u_x)\ge0$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: any finite common spectator cancels when the two bases have equal mass; its mass need not equal the base mass.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Suppose two component signs are opposed. Choose a join state $Z$ and a reversible split $(x,y)$ by T2 in [A2]. Write $x=(u_x,v_x)$ and $y=(u_y,v_y)$. Openness in [A1] permits a sufficiently small nonzero $\delta$ with $x'=(u_x+\delta,v_x)$ and $y'=(u_y-\delta,v_y)$ in their respective charts. Choose the sign of $\delta$ so $\varepsilon_{\Gamma_x}\delta>0$; opposed signs imply $\varepsilon_{\Gamma_y}(-\delta)>0$. Thus [F1] gives $x\prec\prec x'$ and $y\prec\prec y'$. These pairs have the same summed energy and work coordinates and the same represented aggregate composition and mass. [A1, A2, F1, construct]

2.1 If $(x',y')\prec(x,y)$, consistency with $y\prec y'$ gives $(x',y)\prec(x',y')\prec(x,y)$. Cancel the common represented spectator $y$ by [F2] to get $x'\prec x$, contrary to step 1.1. But T1 gives $(x',y')\prec Z$, and the chosen T2 split gives $Z\prec(x,y)$, so transitivity produces exactly this forbidden reverse comparison. Opposed signs are impossible. Every pair has an admitted join, hence one common sign $\varepsilon$ works for the whole family. The affine change $u'=\varepsilon u$ preserves openness and convexity and sends $u=u_x+u_y$ to $u'=\varepsilon u_x+\varepsilon u_y$; its positive orientation describes the same accessibility relation. No physical energy, unit or calibration premise is redefined. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Under T1–T3 and the equal-state reversible split in [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]], if $x\sim_T y$ then $s x\sim_T t y$ for every $s,t>0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The contact and scaling assumptions for tagged states and their joins.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: each equal-state scaled pair is reversibly equivalent to its join, and thermal equivalence is transitive.

## Proof

1.1 Let $x$ be any typed state and $s>0$. The state $z=(1+s)x$ in the scaled type has the equal-state reversible split with fractions $1/(1+s)$ and $s/(1+s)$; its two components are exactly $x$ and $sx$. Thus $(x,sx)$ is reversible with its join, which by definition is $x\sim_T sx$. The same argument gives $y\sim_T ty$. [A1, given]

2.1 Since $x\sim_T y$, symmetry gives $y\sim_T x$. Transitivity with $x\sim_T sx$ yields $y\sim_T sx$; symmetry then gives $sx\sim_T y$. Transitivity with $y\sim_T ty$ now yields $sx\sim_T ty$. [A1, step 1.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on a simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: $A_x$ is defined by $x\prec y$, every state is in its own sector, and each support plane is unique.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: sectors are convex and relatively closed; the collinear implications hold.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every sector has nonempty ambient interior.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: if $w\in\partial A_x$, then $A_w=A_x$.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: if $w$ is in the relative interior of a convex set and $q$ lies in its closure, then $(1-t)w+tq$ lies in the relative interior for every $0\le t<1$.

## Proof

1.1 If $y\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x$. If also $y\in\partial A_x$, [F3] gives equality. Suppose instead $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. If $A_y$ met $\partial A_x$ at $z$, then $z\in A_y$ and [F3] would give $A_z=A_x$. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y\subseteq A_x$, so $A_y=A_x$. But S2 puts $y$ on $\partial A_y$, contradicting $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. Thus $A_y$ avoids $\partial A_x$ and, being a subset of the closed sector $A_x$, lies in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. [A1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Suppose neither $y\in A_x$ nor $x\in A_y$. Choose $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ using [F2]. The segment from $y$ to $z$ lies in $\Gamma_i$ and meets $\partial A_x$ at a point $w$ strictly between its endpoints. By [F3], $A_w=A_x$, so $w\prec z$. The collinear implication in [F1], applied to $w=ty+(1-t)z$, gives $y\prec w\prec z$. Hence every $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ lies in $A_y$. Reversing $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{int}A_y\subseteq A_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Because $A_x$ is full-dimensional by [F2], its affine hull is the ambient space. Fix $w\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. For any $q\in A_x$, relative closedness gives $q\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$, and [F4] puts $(1-t)w+tq$ in $\operatorname{int}A_x$ for every $0\le t<1$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ shows $q\in\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. The reverse inclusion follows because $A_x$ is relatively closed. Hence $A_x=\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$; the same holds for $A_y$. Relative closedness from [F1] therefore extends the two interior inclusions in step 1.2 to $A_x\subseteq A_y$ and $A_y\subseteq A_x$. Equality would put $x\in A_y$, contradicting the supposition. Thus at least one of $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ always holds. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 If $x\prec y$, then $y\in A_x$. If $y$ is a boundary point, step 1.1 gives $A_x=A_y$, hence $x\prec y$ and $y\prec x$. Otherwise step 1.1 gives $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}A_x$, and $x\notin A_y$ because S2 places $x$ on $\partial A_x$. Thus $x\prec\prec y$. Conversely, if $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$, step 1.1 and S2 show $x\notin A_y$, so $x\prec\prec y$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a simple domain and its finite thermal joins satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Let $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$, and let $x$ satisfy $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$. For $0\le\lambda\le1$, write $R_\lambda$ for the compound state $((1-\lambda)x_0,\lambda x_1)$, omitting a zero coefficient at the endpoints. Then there is a unique $\lambda\in(0,1)$ with $R_\lambda\sim x$ in the common accessibility relation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compound axioms A1–A6, thermal-join axioms T1–T3 with the equal-state split, strict strip endpoints, and join closure.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: compounds have the preorder, consistency, positive scaling, splitting, and stability assumptions; CH is not part of this definition.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] and [[lem-tdmath-thermal-scaling-invariance]]: an equal-state split is reversible, thermal equivalence is transitive, and scaling either member of a thermal-equilibrium pair preserves thermal equivalence.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: equal-total signed maps compare by their positive and negative parts; cancellation is valid under A1–A6 without CH.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: every pair of states in each finite join domain is comparable.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$.

1.1 For $0\le\lambda<\mu\le1$, the signed difference $R_\mu-R_\lambda=(\mu-\lambda)(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))$ has positive part $(\mu-\lambda)\iota(x_1)$ and negative part $(\mu-\lambda)\iota(x_0)$. Since $x_0\prec x_1$, positive scaling and [F2] give $R_\lambda\prec R_\mu$. A reverse comparison would, by [F2] and inverse positive scaling, give $x_1\prec x_0$, contrary to strictness. Thus the reference states are strictly ordered by parameter. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For $0<\lambda<1$, [F1] makes $(1-\lambda)x_0$ and $\lambda x_1$ thermally equivalent. By the definition of thermal equivalence, their compound is reversible with its join state. The equal-state split makes $((1-\lambda)x,\lambda x)$ reversible with its join state and with $x$. Both join states belong to the join of two scaled copies of the same simple domain, so [F3] compares them. The endpoint cases use $R_0=x_0$ and $R_1=x_1$ directly. Hence $R_\lambda$ and $x$ are comparable for every $\lambda\in[0,1]$. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Let $L=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:R_\lambda\prec x\}$. The strict endpoint comparison $x_0\prec x$ puts $0$ in $L$. Step 1.1 and transitivity make $L$ downward closed. Let $s=\sup L$. If $s>0$, then $s-1/n\in L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Since $R_{s-1/n}+(1/n)x_1=R_s+(1/n)x_0$, consistency yields $R_s+(1/n)x_0\prec x+(1/n)x_1$. Stability with bases $R_s,x$ and fixed spectators $x_0,x_1$ gives $R_s\prec x$. If $s=0$, this comparison is the given $x_0\prec x$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 If $s<1$, then $s+1/n\notin L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Step 1.2 gives comparability and the definition of $L$ excludes $R_{s+1/n}\prec x$, so $x\prec R_{s+1/n}$. The identity $R_{s+1/n}+(1/n)x_0=R_s+(1/n)x_1$ and stability yield $x\prec R_s$. If $s=1$, the strict strip gives $x\prec R_1$; together with step 2.1 this would imply $x_1\prec x$, contrary to $x\prec\prec x_1$. Thus $s<1$, and step 2.1 and the preceding stability comparison give $R_s\sim x$. [A1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 The equivalence $R_s\sim x$ also excludes $s=0$, because $R_0=x_0$ and $x_0\not\sim x$, and excludes $s=1$ by strictness of $x\prec\prec x_1$. If $R_t\sim x$ for another $t$, transitivity gives $R_s\sim R_t$; step 1.1 then forces $s=t$. Hence the parameter is unique and lies in $(0,1)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated forward-sector and thermal-contact hypotheses; every thermal join remains a simple domain with these hypotheses.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7, S1–S3, and the tagged finite-compound conventions hold, without an assumed CH.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T4 provide simple thermal joins, reversible equilibrium splits, thermal scaling, and a thermal endpoint pair surrounding each state.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-reference-strip-coordinate]]: every state in a strip with strict thermally equivalent endpoints is equivalent to a unique reference mixture with parameter in $(0,1)$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: one-copy comparisons hold on each finite join domain; strict comparison is interior membership, and forward sectors are nested.

[F3] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparison is defined from positive/negative parts; it is translation invariant, additive, and cancellable under A1–A6.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each simple domain has one constant fixed-work energy orientation; arbitrarily close states on a vertical segment are strictly ordered in that orientation.

[F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: a closed bounded subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact.

## Proof

1.1 By T4, the open strips $\Sigma(a,b):=\{x:a\prec\prec x\prec\prec b\}$ with $a\prec\prec b$ and $a\sim_T b$ cover $\Gamma_i$. They are open: by [F2], $a\prec\prec x$ is $x\in\operatorname{int}A_a$, and $x\prec\prec b$ is $x\notin A_b$; the latter set is open because $A_b$ is relatively closed. [A1, A2, F2]

1.2 Let $\Sigma(a,b)$ and $\Sigma(c,d)$ overlap. Their intersection is open. Choose two states $e\prec\prec f$ in a small vertical segment contained in the overlap, using [F4]. Let $s_e,s_f$ be their coordinates in the first strip and $t_e,t_f$ in the second, supplied by [F1]. If $s_f<s_e$, the signed difference $R_{s_e}-R_{s_f}=(s_e-s_f)(\iota(b)-\iota(a))$ and positive scaling and signed compatibility [A1, F3] give $R_{s_f}\prec R_{s_e}$, so $f\prec e$ by the two reference equivalences; if $s_f=s_e$, those references coincide and give $f\sim e$. Both contradict $e\prec\prec f$. Hence $s_f>s_e$, and the same argument gives $t_f>t_e$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 The four reference equivalences give, in signed comparison,
$f-e\sim_s(s_f-s_e)(b-a),\qquad f-e\sim_s(t_f-t_e)(d-c).$
Put $r=(s_f-s_e)/(t_f-t_e)>0$. Additivity and positive scaling in [F3] give $d-c\sim_s r(b-a)$. Applying the same algebra to the equivalences for $e$ gives $c\sim_s a+(s_e-r t_e)(b-a)$. Consequently a state in the second strip with coordinate $t$ has first-chart coordinate $s_e+r(t-t_e)$. The change of chart is affine with strictly positive slope. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The same calculation covers a finite chain of overlapping strips: after each overlap, express the new strip's endpoint states as signed-equivalent affine maps in the existing reference pair. The local strip lemma gives every state $z$ of the added strip a coordinate $s_z\in\mathbb R$ with $\iota(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\iota(a)+s_z\iota(b)$ in the existing chart. Signed addition, positive scaling, translation, and equivalence under negative scaling are valid by [F3]; hence induction along a finite overlap chain gives one such common chart for every state in the union. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Take any finite list of target states in $\Gamma_i$ and join them in order by finitely many straight segments, which lie in $\Gamma_i$ by convexity. The resulting connected path is a finite union of closed bounded segments, hence compact by [F5]. The open strips from step 1.1 cover it, so compactness gives a finite subcover. The intersection graph of those strips meeting the path is connected: otherwise their unions would partition the connected path into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Order a spanning tree from one root strip; each later strip overlaps an earlier one in an open set and can be glued by step 3.1. Thus every target state has a common signed chart $\iota(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\iota(a)+s_z\iota(b)$ with $a\prec\prec b$. [A1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Let $A=\sum_j\alpha_j \iota(x_j)$ and $B=\sum_k\beta_k \iota(y_k)$ have equal total mass $M$, and let $s_j,t_k$ be their common-chart coordinates. If $M=0$, nonnegativity makes both maps empty and reflexivity compares them. Assume $M>0$ and put $L:=M/w_{\Gamma_i}$; both sums of scalar amounts are $L$, since each represented state has mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$. Each state has signed equivalence $\iota(x_j)\sim_s(1-s_j)\iota(a)+s_j\iota(b)$ in the common chart; signed addition, scaling, and splitting [F3] therefore make $A$ and $B$ each signed-equivalent to reference maps $R_{q_A}=(L-q_A)\iota(a)+q_A\iota(b)$ and $R_{q_B}=(L-q_B)\iota(a)+q_B\iota(b)$, where $q_A=\sum_j\alpha_js_j$ and $q_B=\sum_k\beta_kt_k$. If $q_A<q_B$, the signed difference has positive part $(q_B-q_A)\iota(b)$ and negative part $(q_B-q_A)\iota(a)$, so $a\prec b$ and positive scaling compare $R_{q_A}\prec R_{q_B}$ by [F3]. If $q_A=q_B$, the reference maps coincide and reflexivity applies; if $q_B<q_A$, the same argument compares in the reverse direction. Transitivity transfers that comparison to $A,B$. Hence any equal-mass pair is comparable, proving CH. [A1, F3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a simple domain satisfying the forward-sector hypotheses and T1–T4. Let $S$ be the additive extensive entropy supplied by [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] after CH for its finite scaled products is proved by [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]. Then either all pairs of states in $\Gamma$ are thermally equivalent, or there are $x,y$ on one entropy level (equivalently, one adiabat $\partial A_x$ by [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]) with $x\not\sim_T y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The same-type accessibility relation, the thermal relation, the hypotheses in the Statement, and the current entropy representation.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 and S1–S3 hold; the sector theorem supplies a constant fixed-work energy orientation for each type.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T4 hold and thermal equivalence is transitive.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]: every equal-mass finite compound comparison of this simple type is complete.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: under that comparison property, an additive extensive entropy represents every same-type finite-compound comparison.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each simple domain has a constant orientation sign for fixed-work energy comparisons; in coordinates oriented in that sign, sector boundaries are the stated graphs.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-convex-function-local-lipschitz]]: a finite concave entropy is continuous on the open domain.

[F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F6] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: a boundary point $y\in\partial A_x$ has $A_y=A_x$; strict accessibility is interior membership. Together with [F2], this identifies entropy levels with sector boundaries.

[F7] [[lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation]]: T1 and the reversible-split existence in T2 force a common orientation sign; the common affine proof-coordinate change preserves all energy-sum joins and does not redefine physical energy.

## Proof

1.1 Use [F7]'s common mathematical energy orientation for the proof coordinates. Apply [F2] using [F1] after dividing represented coefficient maps by the fixed positive type weight $w_\Gamma$, as specified in [A1]. Multiply the resulting unit-state entropy by $w_\Gamma$ to evaluate represented states; this positive factor preserves all same-type order comparisons. Write $S(x)$ for that represented-state value. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] and additivity imply concavity: for $0<t<1$, accessibility of $(tx,(1-t)y)$ to $tx+(1-t)y$ gives $tS(x)+(1-t)S(y)\le S(tx+(1-t)y)$. By [F3], $S$ is strictly increasing in energy at fixed work coordinate. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F7]

1.2 Fix a work coordinate $v$ and let $J_v:=\{u:(u,v)\in\Gamma\}$, an open interval. The restriction $s_v(u)=S(u,v)$ is finite, concave, continuous by [F4], and strictly increasing by [F3]. For an interior $u$, concavity makes the right secant slopes nonincreasing as the secant endpoint moves right, and the left secant slopes monotone as the endpoint approaches $u$; hence the one-sided derivative limits $s'_{v,+}(u)$ and $s'_{v,-}(u)$ exist. Choose $a<u<b$ in $J_v$: the secants to $a,b$ bound those limits, so they are finite, and concavity gives $s'_-\ge s'_+$. Monotonicity gives nonnegative slopes. If $s'_+(u)=0$, then for every $z>u$ concavity bounds $(s_v(z)-s_v(u))/(z-u)\le s'_+(u)=0$, contradicting strict increase. Thus $s'_-\ge s'_+>0$. Define $\Theta(u,v)=[1/s'_{v,-}(u),1/s'_{v,+}(u)]$, a nonempty compact interval of positive finite reciprocal slopes. [A1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 Suppose the second alternative fails, so each adiabat contains one thermal-equivalence class. By [F1]–[F2], $A_x=\{y:S(y)\ge S(x)\}$. Continuity of $S$ and strict increase in energy at fixed work coordinate imply that every point with $S=\sigma$ has arbitrarily nearby points with larger and smaller entropy; hence each entropy level $E_\sigma=\{x:S(x)=\sigma\}$ is a forward-sector boundary. The supposition makes each $E_\sigma$ lie in one thermal class. Let $R=S(\Gamma)$ and, for each thermal class $C_\alpha$, put $R_\alpha=\{S(x):x\in C_\alpha\}$. These sets partition $R$: two distinct classes cannot share a level under the supposition. The range $R$ is an interval, since any two points of the convex domain are joined by a segment and the continuous entropy takes every intermediate value along it. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6]

2.1 Fix $x=(u_1,v_1)$ and $y=(u_2,v_2)$ of this same simple type, and let $U=u_1+u_2$. The admissible energy splits form the open interval $D=\{w:(U-w,v_1)\in\Gamma,\ (w,v_2)\in\Gamma\}$, which contains $u_2$. Define $g(w)=s_{v_1}(U-w)+s_{v_2}(w)$. For the join state $J(x,y)$, T2 gives an admissible split $q$ whose pair is reversible with the join. For every other split $p$, T1 gives $p\prec J(x,y)\prec q$, so $p\prec q$. The pair states $p,q$ are finite compounds of two copies of this same simple type; [F1]–[F2] and their entropy representation therefore give $g(p)\le g(q)$. Thus $q$ maximizes $g$. If the initial split $x,y$ is reversible with the join, it is equivalent to $q$; entropy representation gives equal entropy, so it too maximizes $g$. Conversely, if $u_2$ maximizes $g$, then $g(u_2)=g(q)$, and [F1]–[F2] make the initial pair reversible with $q$; composing with $q\sim J(x,y)$ shows $x\sim_T y$. For a concave function at an interior point, maximality is equivalent to $g'_+(u_2)\le0\le g'_-(u_2)$: right secants are bounded above by the right derivative and left secants below by the left derivative. Here
$g'_+(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,+}(u_2),\qquad
g'_-(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,-}(u_2).$
The two inequalities are exactly $s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)\le s'_{v_2,-}(u_2)$ and $s'_{v_2,+}(u_2)\le s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)$, which say the positive slope intervals intersect; reciprocal reverses their endpoints, so this is equivalent to $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(y)\ne\varnothing$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 Let $T_\alpha$ be one thermal class. The compact intervals $\Theta(x)$, $x\in T_\alpha$, pairwise intersect by step 2.1. For any finite subfamily, pairwise intersection implies common intersection: the largest left endpoint is no greater than the smallest right endpoint, since the intervals attaining those two endpoints intersect. Fix $x_0\in T_\alpha$; the sets $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(x_0)$ are closed subsets of the compact interval $\Theta(x_0)$ and have the finite-intersection property. Compactness [F5] gives a common point, so $I_\alpha:=\bigcap_{x\in T_\alpha}\Theta(x)$ is a nonempty compact interval. If distinct classes had intersecting common intervals, representatives $x,y$ would have intersecting $\Theta$ intervals and would be thermally equivalent by step 2.1, a contradiction. Thus the intervals $I_\alpha$ for distinct classes are disjoint and strictly ordered on the real line; use this as the order of the classes. [A2, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For each work coordinate $v$, strict continuity of $s_v$ maps the open interval $J_v$ onto an open interval $R_v\subset R$. On $R_v$, the level-to-class map is nondecreasing: as $u$ increases, concavity makes both one-sided slopes nonincreasing, so both endpoints of $\Theta(u,v)$ are nondecreasing. If two such intervals $\Theta$ are disjoint, monotonicity of both endpoints forces the earlier interval to lie strictly below the later one; by step 3.1, this is the class order. The local class maps agree on overlaps of $R_v$ because each entropy level lies in one class. The open intervals $R_v$ cover $R$. Any compact subinterval of $R$ has a finite subcover by these intervals by [F5]; its intersection graph is connected, since otherwise the connected subinterval would be split into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Chaining the local orders through overlaps proves that the class map is nondecreasing on all of $R$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 3.1]

5.1 Fix $\sigma\in R_\alpha$ and $x\in E_\sigma$. T4 gives $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$. Entropy representation gives $S(x_0)<\sigma<S(x_1)$, and their levels belong to the same class $R_\alpha$. The global nondecreasing order from step 4.1 forces every level between them, including an open neighborhood of $\sigma$, into $R_\alpha$. Thus each class set is open in the interval $R$. Since these disjoint open sets partition connected $R$, only one nonempty class exists. Under the supposition, all states are thermally equivalent, proving the dichotomy. [A2, F2, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

Moreover, for every fixed finite composition of scaled copies of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, any two equal-mass states of that same composition are comparable (CH). The conclusion is conditional on the explicitly stated join-coherence and universal-range assumptions C1 and T5.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The forward-sector and contact hypotheses for the whole join-closed family.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 and S1–S3 hold on each member of the family, including finite joins.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T5 hold for every ordered pair in the family, and C1 makes an equilibrated joined state thermally equivalent to each equilibrium constituent.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]: CH holds on every finite scaled product of copies of any simple type in the family.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: under that CH, each simple type and its scaled products have an additive extensive entropy representing accessibility.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-thermal-class-dichotomy]]: for each simple join, either every pair of its states is thermally equivalent or one of its adiabats contains two thermally inequivalent states.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]] and [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: a common adiabat has identical forward sectors; fixed-work accessibility is ordered by energy, and each component adiabat has one state at each work coordinate in its projection.

[F5] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]] and [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]]: signed equivalence is preserved by finite addition and cancellation of common spectators.

[F8] [[lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation]]: T1–T2 and arbitrary-spectator cancellation force a common mathematical energy orientation; the common affine change preserves the join energy-sum rule.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1]–[A2], [F1]–[F5], and [F8].

1.1 Work in [F8]'s common affine mathematical energy orientation, without redefining any physical energy or calibration. Apply [F1] and [F2] to each simple type, including every finite join, using the positive normalization by its fixed weight in [A1]. Throughout, entropy at a state means its represented-state value: $w_\Gamma$ times its unit-point-mass representation. This normalization preserves order and finite scalar amounts. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] makes each resulting entropy concave, since the comparison of a scaled pair with its convex-combination state translates under the representation to the concavity inequality. By [F4], each entropy is strictly increasing with energy at fixed work coordinates. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F8]

1.2 Use T5 to choose $\bar x\in\Gamma_1$ and $\bar y\in\Gamma_2$ with $\bar x\sim_T\bar y$. Let $\phi=J_{12}(\bar x,\bar y)$ and consider its adiabat $\partial A_\phi$. T2 gives every $Z$ on that adiabat at least one split $Z=J_{12}(x_Z,y_Z)$ with $x_Z\sim_T y_Z$. [A2, F4, choose]

2.1 Suppose a join state $Z$ on $\partial A_\phi$ has two distinct equilibrium splits $(x^{(1)},y^{(1)})$ and $(x^{(2)},y^{(2)})$. By the definition of $\sim_T$, both pairs are reversible with $Z$, hence mutually accessible compounds. Their work coordinates are fixed by $Z$ and their total energies equal its energy. If the first-component energies agreed, both component states in the splits would agree, so distinctness forces unequal first-component energies. If $u_{x^{(1)}}<u_{x^{(2)}}$, fixed-work comparison [F4] gives $x^{(1)}\prec\prec x^{(2)}$; conservation of total energy gives $u_{y^{(2)}}<u_{y^{(1)}}$, hence $y^{(2)}\prec\prec y^{(1)}$. Taking $(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)=(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},y^{(2)},y^{(1)})$ gives $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$ because both split compounds are reversible with $Z$. If the first energies occur in the opposite order, swap the two splits and obtain the same calibrator form. Therefore, if no calibrator exists, every $Z\in\partial A_\phi$ has a unique equilibrium split. [A2, F4, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 Assume no calibrator exists. For any equilibrium split $(x_Z,y_Z)$ of $Z\in\partial A_\phi$, reversibility with $Z$ and the common adiabat give $(x_Z,y_Z)\sim(\bar x,\bar y)$ as compounds. By [F1], $x_Z$ and $\bar x$ are comparable; [F4] says their sectors coincide exactly when they are equivalent. If $x_Z\prec\prec\bar x$, pair reversibility gives $(\bar x,\bar y)\prec(x_Z,y_Z)$. Consistency adds $\bar y$ to $x_Z\prec\bar x$, and cancellation [F5] gives $\bar y\prec y_Z$. If $y_Z\prec\bar y$, consistency and the pair comparison instead cancel to give $\bar x\prec x_Z$, a contradiction. Thus $\bar y\prec\prec y_Z$, making a calibrator. The case $\bar x\prec\prec x_Z$ is symmetric: it gives $y_Z\prec\prec\bar y$, again a calibrator. Since neither is allowed under the assumption, $x_Z\sim\bar x$. Adding spectators to the two directions and cancelling by [F5] then gives both $\bar y\prec y_Z$ and $y_Z\prec\bar y$, so $y_Z\sim\bar y$. Thus every split on this adiabat has components in the corresponding component adiabats. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Under the no-calibrator assumption, fix a first-component work coordinate $v_1$ in the projection of $\partial A_{\bar x}$. The boundary-graph result [F4] gives exactly one state $x_*$ on that component adiabat at $v_1$. Every split of a join state on $\partial A_\phi$ with first work coordinate $v_1$ therefore has first component $x_*$. Each split is thermal, so $x_*\sim_T y_Z$ for its second component. T3 makes all such $y_Z$ thermally equivalent, and C1 makes each joined state $J(x_*,y_Z)=Z$ thermally equivalent to $x_*$. Hence all join states on this adiabat over fixed $v_1$ lie in one thermal class. Fixing a second-component work coordinate instead gives the corresponding conclusion for first components. [A2, F4, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $\Omega$ be the open connected work-coordinate projection of $\partial A_\phi$ from [F4]. From any point of $\Omega$, the set reachable by finitely many coordinate-axis segments contained in open boxes in $\Omega$ is relatively open, and its complement is also relatively open; connectedness makes the reachable set all of $\Omega$. Along each such segment, step 4.1 gives equivalence of the corresponding join states; T3 composes these finitely many equivalences. Thus the whole adiabat $\partial A_\phi$ is one thermal class. Since the argument works for every starting join state, every join adiabat is one thermal class. [A2, F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Still assuming no calibrator, apply [F3] to each join system. Its alternative with two thermally inequivalent states on one adiabat is excluded by step 5.1, so all states of each join system are thermally equivalent. For any $x,x'\in\Gamma_1$, use T5 with one allowed second work coordinate to choose $y,y'$ with $x\sim_T y$ and $x'\sim_T y'$. C1 relates each component to its joined state, and all join states are in one thermal class; T3 therefore gives $x\sim_T x'$. The same argument gives one thermal class in $\Gamma_2$. Now take $Z=\phi\in\partial A_\phi$ and a split $(x,y)$ supplied by T2. Choose nonzero sufficiently small $\delta$ so $(u_x+\delta,v_1)\in\Gamma_1$ and $(u_y-\delta,v_2)\in\Gamma_2$, possible because the domains are open. These states form a distinct split of the same $Z$. Since the original split has $x\sim_T y$ and each component type is one thermal class, T3 gives thermal equivalence of the changed pair as well. This contradicts uniqueness of the split from step 2.1. Therefore a calibrator exists. [A2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 5.1, choose]

7.1 Fix a calibrator $x_0\prec\prec x_1$, $y_0\prec\prec y_1$, whose existence is step 6.1. The calibrator says $u\sim v$, so $v-u=(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))-(\iota(y_1)-\iota(y_0))$ is equivalent to zero; translation and cancellation [F5] give $(\iota(x_1)-\iota(x_0))\sim_s(\iota(y_1)-\iota(y_0))$. Its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy, so [F2] makes them equivalent. Hence $\iota(x)\sim_s(1-s(x))\iota(x_0)+s(x)\iota(x_1)$; the same argument applies to states of the second type. These are formal signed maps when a coefficient lies outside $[0,1]$. 8.1 For a state pair $(x,y)$, put $\lambda=(s(x)+t(y))/2$ and $\delta=(s(x)-t(y))/2$. ## Statement

Let $I$ be a nonempty set of primitive simple-system labels containing a distinguished meter label $m$. Assume every finite separated product is explicitly represented by its finitely many tagged elementary factors; positive scaling and finite product are the only identifications. Suppose the join-closed family satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]], and fix a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Then one can choose, for every $i\in I$, an additive constant and positive scale for its same-type entropy so that

$$S\big((t_1i_1,x_1),\ldots,(t_ni_n,x_n)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^n t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$$

is additive, extensive, and characterizes every same-composition comparison on every finite separated product. No conclusion is asserted for transitions that change composition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The explicit finite-factor family, common contact branch, strict meter pair, and Axiom of Choice.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function; it selects the reference states, entropy representatives, and calibrator data used below.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]]: for each pair of simple types in the join-closed family, strict calibrator endpoints exist and their reversible pair relation identifies the two reference increments in signed comparison.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: once a type and its scaled products have CH, a finite real additive extensive entropy represents their equal-mass comparisons.

[F3] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparison is translation-invariant and additive, agrees with ordinary comparison on nonnegative equal-mass maps, and permits common-spectator cancellation.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Use the positive type normalization in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] whenever invoking [F2]; state entropies evaluate represented maps $\iota(x)$, and their unit-label entropy density is $S_i(x)/w_{\Gamma_i}$. Apply [F2] to the meter type and choose its entropy $S_m$ so $S_m(z_0)=0$ and $S_m(z_1)=1$. Set the meter reference to $r_m=z_0$, and use [A1] to choose a reference state $r_i$ and one same-type entropy representative for every $i\ne m$. For each $i\ne m$, use [F1] to choose calibrator states $a_i,b_i\in\Gamma_i$ and $c_i,d_i\in\Gamma_m$ such that $a_i\prec\prec b_i$, $c_i\prec\prec d_i$, and $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$; also choose $r_i\in\Gamma_i$.
